name: Near-simultaneous trades
brief:
A surveillance check counts pairs of trades that happen within `d` milliseconds of each other. The input comes as one string, as a judge would send it:

- the first line holds `n` and `d`, separated by a space;
- the second line holds the `n` trade times, sorted from earliest to latest, separated by spaces (it may be missing when `n` is 0).

Write `solve_near_trades(text)`, which returns, as a string, the number of pairs of positions `i < j` with `times[j] - times[i] <= d`. Expect extra spaces and a trailing newline.

Example. For the input `"5 2\n1 2 4 5 9\n"` the close pairs are 1 with 2, 2 with 4, and 4 with 5. So the answer is `"3"`.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ times, sorted, each a whole number between $0$ and $10^9$; $0 \le d \le 10^9$.
$O(n)$ time after reading is the target. Checking every pair is too slow.
Each test has its own 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Read every token with `text.split()`. Then move a right pointer along the times and keep a left pointer on the earliest time still within `d` of it.

examples.note: Three neighbours sit within 2 ms; 2 with 5 is 3 ms apart and misses.
Equal times are 0 ms apart, so all three pairs count.

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Both pointers only move forward: as the right time grows, the earliest close time can only move later.
Each right end adds `right - left` pairs, and an `n` of 0 means the second line may not exist.
Reading is $O(n)$ and so is the sweep.
